title: Latin for Beginners
author: Benjamin L. D'Ooge
licenseEvidence: Project Gutenberg eBook #18251, marked public domain in the USA; title page reads 'Copyright, 1909, 1911 by Benjamin L. D'Ooge', Ginn and Company. Published before 1930, so public domain in the USA.
description: Benjamin D'Ooge's classic 1909 first-year Latin course, a favorite of classical homeschoolers for middle and high school. Each day brings a short grammar point, a vocabulary list, and two sets of sentences to translate, Latin to English and English to Latin, with stories of Perseus, Hercules, and a Roman boy in Caesar's army along the way. The full book is free to read online.
includes: 124 lessons in 13 units covering all 79 lessons, the 8 reviews, Part I on pronunciation, and the reading selections
A link to the exact lesson and its special vocabulary in the free online book
24 reading lessons: The Labors of Hercules and the story of Publius Cornelius Lentulus
Short translation and grammar questions with answers every day

lessons.title: To the Student: What Is Latin?
steps: Read the introduction together and find Latium and Rome on a map
List five English words you use that come from Latin
Answer the review questions at the end out loud
questions: Which district of Italy gave Latin its name?
Name two modern languages that grew out of Latin.
Which people became Rome's teachers in art and learning?
answers: Any two of Italian, Spanish, French
lessons.notes: A gentle first day: no memorizing yet, just why Latin matters.

lessons.title: Part I: The Alphabet and the Sounds of the Letters
steps: Read §§ 1–7 and say each example word after the parent
Practice the long and short vowels, then the six diphthongs
Drill the tricky consonants: c, g, i consonant, v, and s
questions: How is c always pronounced in Latin?
How is v pronounced?
What English sound does the diphthong ae make?
answers: Like c in cat (a hard k)
lessons.notes: The book says these sounds are best learned by ear; read them aloud together.

lessons.title: Part I: Syllables, Quantity, and Accent
steps: Read §§ 8–16 on dividing syllables, long and short syllables, and accent
Divide the words of the ant passage (§ 10) into syllables and read it aloud
Mark the accent on five words using the penult rule
questions: How many syllables does a Latin word have?
Where is a word of two syllables accented?
What is the syllable next to the last called?
answers: As many as it has vowels and diphthongs

lessons.title: Part I: How to Read Latin — Excelsior
steps: Read § 17 on reading in phrases, not word by word
Read Longfellow's "Excelsior" one stanza at a time, first English, then Latin
Pick one Latin stanza and practice reading it smoothly
questions: Which syllable must you watch to get the accent right?
What one Latin word ends every stanza?

units.title: Unit 1: First Principles and the First Declension (Lessons I–VIII)

lessons.title: Lesson I: First Principles — Subject, Predicate, and Object
steps: Read §§ 19–21 on subject, predicate, object, and the copula
Pronounce the eight Latin sentences in § 22 and name the subject, verb, and object of each
Notice which English words (the, a, my) Latin leaves out
questions: What does agricola mean?
Translate: Iūlia aquam portat.
Does Latin have a word for "the"?

lessons.title: Lesson II: Inflection, Number, and Personal Endings
steps: Learn the 13 nouns in § 26 and write the plural of each
Learn the rule for verb agreement and the endings -t and -nt
Do Exercises I (English to Latin) and II (Latin to English)
questions: What is the plural of puella?
Translate: Nautae pugnant.
Write in Latin: The farmer labors.

lessons.title: Lesson III: Declension — Nominative, Genitive, Accusative
steps: Read § 32 and see how endings, not word order, show subject and object
Memorize the table in § 33 for domina, singular and plural
Do the exercise in § 34: give number, case, and use of each form
questions: Translate: Fīliam domina amat.
What case is dominārum, and what does it mean?
Give the accusative plural of silva.

lessons.title: Lesson IV: Diana and Latona — Subject, Object, Possessor
steps: Learn the three rules in §§ 36–38 and the special vocabulary
Translate Exercise I about Diana; then put Exercise II into Latin
Answer the conversation questions (§ 40) in Latin
questions: Translate: Diāna est fīlia Lātōnae.
Write in Latin: Latona's daughter carries arrows.
What question does the genitive answer?
answers: Diana is the daughter of Latona

lessons.title: Lesson V: The Dative and the Indirect Object
steps: Read §§ 41–45 and form the dative of the nine nouns in § 42
Learn the special vocabulary; translate Exercise I and point out the indirect objects
Put Exercise II into Latin, keeping the book's word order
questions: Give the dative singular and plural of nauta.
Translate: Puella Diānae corōnam dat.
Write in Latin: The farmer gives his daughter water.
answers: The girl gives a wreath to Diana

lessons.title: Lesson VI: The Ablative, Prepositions, and Adjectives
steps: Read about the ablative (§§ 48–53) and translate the prepositional phrases in § 53
Read about attributive and predicate adjectives (§§ 54–55)
Learn the vocabulary and read the dialogue of Julia and Galba as a play
questions: Write in Latin: out of the forests.
How do you answer "yes" to Pugnatne nauta? in Latin?
Translate: Fīlia mea nōn est sōla.

lessons.title: Lesson VII: The First (Ā-) Declension and Gender
steps: Study the full table of domina in § 57 and the idea of the base
Decline pugna, terra, lūna, ancilla, corōna, īnsula, silva
Translate Exercise I about the farmer's daughter; put Exercise II into Latin
questions: What gender is agricola, and why?
Translate: Agricola cum fīliā in casā habitat.
Write in Latin: The farmer praises the good dinner.
answers: Masculine, because it names a male
The farmer lives in a cottage with his daughter

lessons.title: Lesson VIII: Adjective Agreement and Latin Word Order
steps: Decline domina bona together, then puella mala and ancilla parva
Learn the -ābus forms of dea and fīlia
Read § 68 on word order, then translate the exercise and name the emphatic words
questions: Give the dative plural of dea.
Translate: Longa est Italia, nōn lāta.
Which place in a Latin sentence is most emphatic?

lessons.title: Review I: Vocabulary and Grammar through Lesson VIII
steps: Give the English for every word in § 502, then the Latin for the list in § 503
Underline the words you missed and drill only those
Answer the review questions (§ 504) aloud and fill out the first-declension summary (§ 505)
questions: Give the English of sagitta.
Give the Latin for "pleasing."
What is the gender rule for the first declension?
answers: Feminine, unless the noun names a male
lessons.notes: Do not look anything up until you have gone through the whole list once.

units.title: Unit 2: The Second Declension, Adjectives, and Pronouns (Lessons IX–XVII)

lessons.title: Lesson IX: The Second (O-) Declension — dominus and pīlum
steps: Learn the declension of dominus and pīlum (§ 73) and write them beside domina
Read the general rules in § 74 and the rule for the predicate noun
Learn the vocabulary, read the dialogue of Galba and Marcus, and answer § 78 in Latin
questions: Give the vocative singular of dominus.
What is the nominative plural of pīlum?
Translate: Lēgātus est Sextus.

lessons.title: Lesson X: Masculine and Neuter Adjectives; Apposition
steps: Decline dominus bonus and pīlum bonum, then bellum longum and equus parvus
Learn the rule of apposition (§ 81) with the Lesbia examples
Translate the phrases and sentences of Exercise I; put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Rhēnus est in Germāniā, patriā meā.
Write in Latin: Mark, where is Lesbia, the maidservant?
In what case does an appositive stand?
answers: The Rhine is in Germany, my fatherland
The same case as the noun it explains

lessons.title: Lesson XI: Adjectives of the First and Second Declensions
steps: Decline bonus, bona, bonum across the page in all three genders
Learn nauta bonus and see why noun and adjective endings can differ
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: How do you say "a good sailor" in Latin?
Translate: Fāma nautārum bonōrum est clāra.
Write in Latin: Sextus, where is my helmet?
answers: The fame of the good sailors is great (famous)

lessons.title: Lesson XII: Nouns in -ius and -ium — Germānia
steps: Learn the genitive and vocative of fīlius and praesidium (§§ 87–89)
Translate the phrases in Exercise I
Read and translate the short passage about Germany
questions: Give the genitive singular of praesidium.
Give the vocative of fīlius.
Translate: Populus Germāniae bellum amat.
answers: The people of Germany love war

lessons.title: Lesson XIII: Nouns and Adjectives in -er and -ir — Italia
steps: Decline puer, ager, and vir; note which keep the e
Decline together vir līber and puella pulchra
Learn the vocabulary, read the passage on Italy, and read the dialogue of Marcus and Cornelius
questions: Give the genitive singular of ager.
What is the base of puer?
Translate: Pulchra est terra Italia.

lessons.title: Lesson XIV: The Possessive Adjective Pronouns
steps: Learn meus, tuus, suus, noster, vester and the vocative mī
Read § 98 on when to use tuus or vester and how suus points back to the subject
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: How do you say "O my son"?
Translate: Nostra castra sunt vestra.
Write in Latin: The camp is mine, but the weapons are yours (one person).
answers: Castra sunt mea, sed tēla sunt tua

lessons.title: Lesson XV: The Ablative Denoting With — The Romans Prepare for War
steps: Read the four kinds of "with" (§ 100) and learn the rules for cause, means, accompaniment, and manner
Find each ablative use in the English passage of § 106
Learn the vocabulary; translate "The Romans Prepare for War" and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Which ablatives never take cum?
Translate: Iūlia est cum Sextō.
Write in Latin: The legionaries are armed with long spears.

lessons.title: Lesson XVI: The Nine Irregular Adjectives
steps: Learn the list of nine (alius, alter, ūnus, ūllus, nūllus, sōlus, tōtus, uter, neuter) and their -īus, -ī endings
Learn the idioms alter … alter, alius … alius, aliī … aliī
Translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Give the genitive singular of nūllus.
Translate: Aliī gladiōs, aliī scūta portant.
Write in Latin: in neither cottage

lessons.title: Lesson XVII: The Demonstrative is, ea, id
steps: Decline is, ea, id and learn its use for he, she, it, they
Study when to use suus and when to use eius or eōrum (§ 116)
Learn the vocabulary; put the English exercise into Latin and read the dialogue
questions: What is the genitive singular of is?
Write in Latin: Galba calls his (own) son.
Write in Latin: Galba calls his son (another man's).

lessons.title: Review II: Lessons IX–XVII
steps: Give the English of the words in § 506, then the Latin of the list in § 507
Drill the words you missed
Answer the review questions and fill out the second-declension summary
questions: Give the English of lōrīca.
Give the Latin for "son."
How can you tell whether an -er adjective goes like līber or like pulcher?
answers: By the feminine and neuter forms (lībera, pulchra)

units.title: Unit 3: The Verb in the Active Voice (Lessons XVIII–XXVI)

lessons.title: Lesson XVIII: Conjugation — Present, Imperfect, and Future of sum
steps: Read about tense, mood, and person (§§ 119–122) and learn the active personal endings
Memorize sum, eram, and erō in all persons
Learn the vocabulary, read the dialogue of Sextus and Marcus, and do the exercise in § 125
questions: What are the six active personal endings?
Translate: Eritisne mox in lūdō?
Write in Latin: Lately I was wretched.
answers: Will you soon be in school?

lessons.title: Lesson XIX: The Four Conjugations — Present of amō and moneō
steps: Learn the four present infinitives and how to find the present stem
Conjugate amō and moneō in the present, then the verbs in § 129
Parse the forms in Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: What is the present stem of monēre?
Translate: vidēmus
Write in Latin: they order

lessons.title: Lesson XX: The Imperfect of amō and moneō — Niobe and Her Children
steps: Learn the tense sign -bā- and conjugate amābam and monēbam
Translate the forms in Exercise I; put Exercise II into Latin
Learn the vocabulary and read the first part of the Niobe story
questions: What is the tense sign of the imperfect?
Translate: dēlēbāmus
How many sons and daughters did Niobe have?

lessons.title: Lesson XXI: The Future of amō and moneō — Niobe (Concluded)
steps: Learn the tense sign -bi- and conjugate amābō and monēbō
Translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
Learn the vocabulary and finish the story of Niobe
questions: Translate: vidēbimus
Write in Latin: they will care for
Which two children of Latona punished Niobe's children?

lessons.title: Lesson XXII: Review of Verbs; the Dative with Adjectives — Cornelia
steps: Review the present, imperfect, and future of sum and the verbs in § 129, out loud and in writing
Learn the rule for the dative with adjectives and the seven adjectives in § 144
Translate Exercise I, put Exercise II into Latin, and read the first part of Cornelia and her Jewels
questions: Translate: Gallī cōpiīs Rōmānīs inimīcī erant.
Write in Latin: The sacrifices were pleasing to Latona.
Who were Cornelia's two sons?
answers: The Gauls were hostile to the Roman forces

lessons.title: Lesson XXIII: The Present of regō and audiō — Cornelia (Concluded)
steps: Conjugate regō and audiō in the present and note where -i- and -u- appear
Inflect agō, dīcō, dūcō, mittō, mūniō, reperiō, veniō
Translate Exercise I, put Exercise II into Latin, and finish the Cornelia story
questions: Translate: Cuius castra mūniunt?
Write in Latin: they hear
What did Cornelia call her jewels?

lessons.title: Lesson XXIV: The Imperfect of regō and audiō; Dative with Special Verbs
steps: Conjugate regēbam and audiēbam and compare them with monēbam
Learn the seven intransitive verbs that take the dative (crēdō, faveō, noceō, pāreō, persuādeō, resistō, studeō)
Translate the exercises in §§ 152 and 155
questions: Translate: mūniēbāmus
Translate: Tiberius et Gāius Cornēliae pārēbant.
Which case does resistō take?

lessons.title: Lesson XXV: The Future of regō and audiō
steps: Learn the future tense sign -ā-/-ē- and conjugate regam and audiam
Translate Exercise I and notice how dīcet differs from dīcit
Put the sentences of Exercise II into Latin, using the dative with special verbs
questions: Translate: mittēmus
Write in Latin: I shall come.
Write in Latin: A good slave obeys his master.

lessons.title: Lesson XXVI: Verbs in -iō; the Imperative Mood
steps: Conjugate capiō in the present, imperfect, and future; then faciō, fugiō, iaciō, rapiō
Learn the imperative singular and plural, including dīc, dūc, fac
Translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Give the imperative plural of audiō.
Translate: Este bonī, puerī.
Write in Latin: The goddess will seize her arms.

lessons.title: Review III: Lessons XVIII–XXVI
steps: Give the English of the words in § 510 and the Latin of the list in § 511, with infinitives
Drill the words you missed
Answer the review questions and conjugate one verb of each conjugation in three tenses
questions: Give the English of trīstitia.
Give the Latin for "find" with its infinitive.
What is the tense sign of the future in the first two conjugations?

units.title: Unit 4: The Passive Voice and the Perfect System (Lessons XXVII–XXXVI)

lessons.title: Lesson XXVII: The Passive Voice of amō and moneō — Perseus and Andromeda
steps: Learn the passive personal endings (-r, -ris, -tur, -mur, -minī, -ntur)
Conjugate amor and moneor in the present, imperfect, and future; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
Learn the vocabulary and read the first part of Perseus and Andromeda
questions: Translate: vocābātur
Write in Latin: we are praised
Which god sent the sea monster to Aethiopia?

lessons.title: Lesson XXVIII: The Passive of regō and audiō — Perseus (Continued)
steps: Learn the passive of regō and audiō in three tenses; note regeris, not regiris
Translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
Learn the vocabulary and read what the oracle answered Cepheus
questions: Translate: mittentur
Write in Latin: it is said
What did the oracle tell Cepheus to give the monster?

lessons.title: Lesson XXIX: The Passive of -iō Verbs; Infinitive and Imperative
steps: Learn the passive of capiō in three tenses
Learn the present infinitives, active and passive, and the passive imperative
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Give the present passive infinitive of mittō.
Give the present passive infinitive of audiō.
Translate: Mōnstrum est validum, tamen superābitur.
answers: The monster is strong, yet it will be overcome

lessons.title: Lesson XXX: Synopses; the Ablative Denoting From
steps: Practice synopses (§ 177) of rapiō, mūniō, doceō, and laudō in several persons
Learn the rules for place from which, separation, and the personal agent; compare sagittā with ā Diānā
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Fera ā Diānā necātur.
Write in Latin: They were without food.
Which ablative needs ā or ab: means or personal agent?
answers: The wild beast is killed by Diana

lessons.title: Lesson XXXI: Principal Parts; the Perfect System of sum
steps: Learn what the four principal parts are and how to find the perfect stem
Memorize the perfect endings and conjugate fuī, fueram, fuerō
Learn the vocabulary, read the dialogue about Sextus's boat, and do the exercise in § 189
questions: What are the principal parts of sum (first three)?
Translate: Ubi fuistis?
Write in Latin: They had been in school.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXII: The Perfect Active in All Four Conjugations — Perseus (Continued)
steps: Read § 190 on the two meanings of the perfect and when a story uses perfect or imperfect
Learn the perfects amāvī, monuī, rēxī, cēpī, audīvī and the principal parts in § 192
Learn the vocabulary and read how Cepheus chained Andromeda to the rocks
questions: Give the perfect (third principal part) of mittō.
Translate: Perseus ad terram dēscendit.
What did Cepheus promise Perseus if he killed the monster?
answers: Perseus came down to the earth

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIII: The Pluperfect and Future Perfect Active; Perfect Infinitive
steps: Inflect the pluperfect (-eram) and future perfect (-erō) of the five model verbs
Form the perfect active infinitive with -isse
Translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: discesserāmus
Give the perfect active infinitive of videō.
Write in Latin: they have obeyed

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIV: Review of the Active Voice — Perseus (Concluded)
steps: Learn the table of how each active tense is formed (§ 197)
Give quick synopses of five verbs from § 198 and learn the perfects in § 199
Learn the vocabulary and read the end of Perseus and Andromeda, explaining each perfect and imperfect
questions: How is the pluperfect active formed?
Give the perfect of reperiō.
Translate: Perseus mōnstrum interfēcit.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXV: The Passive Perfects; Perfect Passive and Future Active Infinitives
steps: Learn the fourth principal part and the participial stem
Form the perfect, pluperfect, and future perfect passive with sum, making the participle agree
Translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Puellae laudātae sunt.
Give the future active infinitive of amō.
Write in Latin: the field had been laid waste

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVI: Review of Principal Parts; Prepositions; Yes-or-No Questions
steps: Learn the full principal parts of every verb so far (§ 208)
Learn which prepositions take the ablative and which the accusative, and the two meanings of in
Learn -ne, nōnne, and num; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Which answer does a question with nōnne expect?
Give the four principal parts of dūcō.
Write in Latin: He isn't coming, is he?

lessons.title: Review IV: Lessons XXVII–XXXVI
steps: Give the English of the words in § 513; translate the list in § 514 with genitives, genders, and principal parts
Drill the words you missed
Answer the review questions on the passive voice and the perfect system
questions: Give the English of perīculum.
Give the Latin for "suddenly."
What are the passive personal endings?

units.title: Unit 5: possum, Relatives, and the Third Declension (Lessons XXXVII–XLIV)

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVII (Part 1): possum and the Uses of the Infinitive
steps: Learn the principal parts and indicative of possum (§ 495)
Learn the accusative subject of the infinitive, the complementary infinitive, and the infinitive as a noun
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Diū sine aquā vīvere nōn potestis.
Write in Latin: To see is to believe.
In what case is the subject of an infinitive?
answers: You cannot live long without water

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVII (Part 2): The Faithless Tarpeia
steps: Read the Tarpeia story aloud in Latin, a sentence at a time
Translate it, explaining why cōnsilium cēpērunt is perfect while the earlier verbs are imperfect
Narrate the first half of the story in English
questions: Where had the Romans fled from the Sabines?
What did Tarpeia carry to the Roman troops every day?
What did Tarpeia long for?

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVIII (Part 1): The Relative Pronoun quī, quae, quod
steps: Read § 219 on simple, compound, and complex sentences
Decline quī, quae, quod and compare it with is, ea, id
Learn the rule for agreement of the relative and explain the two examples in § 223
questions: Give the dative plural of quī.
Translate: Rōmānī interfēcērunt fēminam quae capta est.
With what must a relative agree in gender and number?
answers: The Romans killed the woman who was captured

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVIII (Part 2): The Interrogative Pronoun — Tarpeia (Concluded)
steps: Learn quis, quid (pronoun) and quī, quae, quod (adjective)
Translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
Read the end of the Tarpeia story
questions: Translate: Quī vir eōs dūcit?
Write in Latin: What victory will you announce?
How did the Sabines kill Tarpeia?
answers: They threw their shields on her

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIX: The Third Declension — Consonant Stems (Class I)
steps: Read about bases and stems (§§ 230–232)
Decline prīnceps, mīles, lapis, rēx, iūdex, virtūs; then dux, eques, pedes, pēs
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Give the genitive singular of mīles.
How do you find the base of a third-declension noun?
Translate: Pedēs mīlitum lapidibus vulnerābantur.
answers: The soldiers' feet were wounded by stones

lessons.title: Lesson XL: Consonant Stems (Class II) — cōnsul, legiō, ōrdō, pater
steps: Decline cōnsul, legiō, ōrdō, and pater
Note how -ōn-, -in-, and -tr- stems change in the nominative
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Give the genitive singular of legiō.
Give the accusative plural of pater.
Write in Latin: Who has seen my father today?

lessons.title: Lesson XLI: Neuter Consonant Stems — flūmen, tempus, opus, caput
steps: Decline flūmen, tempus, opus, and caput
Apply the neuter rules of § 74 (nominative and accusative alike, plural in -a)
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Give the nominative plural of tempus.
Translate: Rōma est in rīpīs flūminis magnī.
Write in Latin: To save the fatherland was a great task.
answers: Rome is on the banks of a great river

lessons.title: Lesson XLII: Review Lesson — Terror Cimbricus
steps: Review the paradigms of prīnceps, cōnsul, and flūmen (§§ 233, 236, 238)
Translate the story of the Cimbri and Teutons and Marius
Decline every third-declension noun you find in the story
questions: Who was called back from Africa to save Rome?
What was Marius called after the victory?
Translate: Servāte patriam!

lessons.title: Lesson XLIII: The Third Declension — I-Stems
steps: Learn which nouns are i-stems (§ 241) and how they differ from consonant stems
Decline caedēs, hostis, urbs, cliēns, then īnsigne, animal, calcar
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Give the genitive plural of urbs.
Give the nominative plural of animal.
Translate: Alia animālia terram, alia mare amant.
answers: Some animals love the land, others the sea

lessons.title: Lesson XLIV: Irregular Nouns and Gender in the Third Declension — The First Bridge over the Rhine
steps: Decline vīs and iter
Learn the gender rules in § 247 and give the gender of the nouns in § 248
Learn the vocabulary; translate the Rhine bridge story and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: What gender is mōns?
Give the genitive singular of iter.
Why did the Germans flee when they saw the bridge?
answers: They were struck with terror, for no bridge had been seen on the Rhine before

lessons.title: Review V: Lessons XXXVII–XLIV
steps: Give the English of the words in § 517; translate the list in § 518 with genitives, genders, and principal parts
Drill the words you missed
Answer the review questions on possum, the infinitive, the relative, and the third declension
questions: Give the English of flūmen.
Give the Latin for "never."
What gender is a third-declension noun ending in -or?

units.title: Unit 6: Fourth and Fifth Declensions; Pronouns (Lessons XLV–LII)

lessons.title: Lesson XLV: Adjectives of the Third Declension — The Romans Invade the Enemy's Country
steps: Learn the three classes: ācer, ācris, ācre; omnis, omne; pār
Decline vir ācer, ager omnis, and proelium pār; note the ablative in -ī
Learn the vocabulary; translate the invasion story and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Give the ablative singular of omnis.
Translate: Fortūna fortibus semper favet.
Who was among the captives?

lessons.title: Lesson XLVI: The Fourth (U-) Declension
steps: Decline adventus and cornū; note the feminines domus and manus
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I
Put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Give the genitive singular of adventus.
Translate: Ante adventum Caesaris
Write in Latin: I trained my horse with my own hands.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVII: Expressions of Place; the Locative; domus — Daedalus and Icarus
steps: Learn the rules for place to which, from which, and where, and the exceptions for towns, domus, and rūs
Learn the locative (Rōmae, Corinthī, domī) and the declension of domus (§ 468)
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and read the start of Daedalus and Icarus
questions: Write in Latin: Galba lives at Rome.
Write in Latin: Galba hastens home.
Why could Daedalus not escape from Crete at first?
answers: The king would not let him go and the sea blocked his flight
lessons.notes: Exercise II (English to Latin) can be done the next day if time runs short.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVIII: The Fifth (Ē-) Declension; the Ablative of Time
steps: Decline diēs and rēs
Learn the rule for the ablative of time (prīmā lūce, merīdiē, hieme)
Learn the vocabulary; translate Galba the Farmer, put Exercise II into Latin, and continue Daedalus
questions: Give the genitive singular of rēs.
Translate: Hieme agricola eōs in lūdum mittit.
What did Daedalus make out of feathers?
answers: In winter the farmer sends them to school

lessons.title: Lesson XLIX: Personal and Reflexive Pronouns — Daedalus and Icarus (Concluded)
steps: Learn the eight classes of pronouns, then decline ego, tū, nōs, vōs, and suī
Practice reflexives (videō mē, sē videt) and forms like mēcum, nōbīscum
Learn the vocabulary; translate the exercises and finish the Daedalus story
questions: Give the dative of ego.
Write in Latin: The boy sees himself.
Why did Icarus fall into the sea?
answers: He flew too near the sun and his wings were burned

lessons.title: Lesson L: ipse and īdem — How Horatius Held the Bridge
steps: Learn ipse (-self, very) and how it differs from the reflexive suī
Decline īdem, eadem, idem and note how m becomes n before d
Learn the vocabulary; translate the exercises and the start of the Horatius story
questions: Translate: Caesar ipse scūtum ēripuit.
Write in Latin: in the same city
Who came with an army to help Tarquin the Proud?

lessons.title: Lesson LI: The Demonstratives hic, iste, ille — Horatius (Continued)
steps: Learn hic, haec, hoc and the forms of iste and ille
Study the model sentences (§ 293): this near me, that near you, that over there
Learn the vocabulary; translate the German chieftain's speech, Exercise II, and the next part of Horatius
questions: Give the genitive singular of hic.
Translate: Iste equus est validus, sed ille est īnfīrmus.
How many comrades stood with Horatius at the bridge?
answers: That horse of yours is strong, but that one yonder is weak

lessons.title: Lesson LII: The Indefinite Pronouns — Horatius (Concluded)
steps: Learn quis, aliquis, quīdam, quisquam, and quisque and when each is used
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
Read how Horatius held the bridge alone and swam to safety
questions: Translate: sī quis
Write in Latin: Each one was praising his own work.
What did the Roman people set up in honor of Horatius?
answers: A statue in a public place

lessons.title: Review VI: Lessons XLV–LII
steps: Give the English of the words in § 521 and translate the list in § 522
Drill the words you missed
Answer the review questions on the fourth and fifth declensions, place, time, and pronouns
questions: Give the English of exercitus.
Give the Latin for "hope."
How do you say "at home" in Latin?

units.title: Unit 7: Comparison — The Labors of Hercules (Lessons LIII–LVI)

lessons.title: Lesson LIII: Regular Comparison of Adjectives
steps: Learn the endings -ior, -ius and -issimus, and decline clārior
Compare longus, fortis, recēns, and the -er adjectives ācer, pulcher, miser
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Compare clārus (all three degrees).
Give the superlative of pulcher.
Write in Latin: Of all birds the eagle is the swiftest.

lessons.title: Reading Matter: How to Translate; The Labors of Hercules
steps: Read the six suggestions for translating and the section on the parts of a sentence
Read the English summary of the life of Hercules
Practice the method on one sentence from an earlier story: find subject, verb, and object first
questions: What gives you the "backbone" of a Latin sentence?
For how many years did Hercules serve Eurystheus?
Which goddess hated Hercules all his life?
answers: The nominatives and accusatives with the verb (subject, verb, object)

lessons.title: Reading LIII: The Infant Hercules and the Serpents
steps: Translate the selection, using the six-step method
Find the comparatives and superlatives in it
Tell the story back in English
questions: Who sent the serpents?
On what were Hercules and his brother sleeping?
What did the frightened brother do?
answers: He called loudly for his mother

lessons.title: Lesson LIV: Irregular Comparison (-lis Adjectives); Ablative with Comparatives
steps: Learn the six -lis adjectives with superlatives in -limus (facillimus, simillimus …)
Learn the ablative with comparatives without quam (Nihil est clārius sōle)
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Give the superlative of facilis.
Translate: Nihil pulchrius urbe Rōmā vīdī.
Write in Latin (without quam): The eagle is not slower than the horse.
answers: I have seen nothing more beautiful than the city of Rome

lessons.title: Reading LIV: Hercules Conquers the Minyae; the Delphic Oracle
steps: Translate the two short sections
List every superlative you find
Narrate why Hercules went to Delphi
questions: What did the Minyae demand from Thebes every year?
What did King Creon give Hercules after the victory?
Who gave advice at the oracle of Delphi?

lessons.title: Lesson LV: Irregular Comparison (Continued); plūs
steps: Learn bonus–melior–optimus, magnus–maior–maximus, malus–peior–pessimus, multus–plūs–plūrimus, parvus–minor–minimus
Learn the double superlatives (extrēmus, īnfimus/īmus, postrēmus, suprēmus/summus) and decline plūs
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Compare malus.
Give the comparative and superlative of parvus.
Write in Latin: Slavery is worse than death.

lessons.title: Reading LV: Hercules Serves Eurystheus; the Nemean Lion
steps: Translate the selection
Find the connecting relative (Quae ubi audīvit) and explain it
Tell how Hercules killed the lion
questions: To which king did Hercules give himself as a slave?
Why could arrows not stop the lion?
What did Hercules wear afterward?

lessons.title: Lesson LVI: Irregular Comparison (Concluded); Ablative of Measure of Difference
steps: Learn citerior, interior, prior, propior, ulterior and their superlatives
Learn the ablative of the measure of difference (multō, paulō, nihilō)
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Haec via est multō lātior quam illa.
Give the superlative of prior.
Write in Latin: Your horse is a little swifter than mine.
answers: This road is much wider than that one
Tuus equus est paulō celerior quam meus

lessons.title: Reading LVI: Slaying the Lernaean Hydra
steps: Translate the selection
Notice the second connecting relative (Quod ubi vīdit)
Draw or describe the Hydra from the Latin
questions: How many heads did the Hydra have?
How did Hercules stop new heads from growing?
What did he do with the last head?
answers: He burned the necks with fire
He put it under a huge rock, because it was immortal

units.title: Unit 8: Adverbs, Numerals, Deponents — Hercules Concluded (Lessons LVII–LX)

lessons.title: Lesson LVII: Formation and Comparison of Adverbs
steps: Learn how adverbs are made with -ē, -iter, and -ter, and compared
Memorize the irregular adverbs (bene, melius, optimē; diū; magnopere; parum; prope; saepe)
Learn the vocabulary; form the adverbs in § 324, translate Exercise I, and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Form the adverb from fortis.
Compare the adverb bene.
Translate: Rōmānī saepius quam hostēs vīcērunt.
answers: The Romans won more often than the enemy

lessons.title: Reading LVII: The Arcadian Stag and the Erymanthian Boar
steps: Translate the selection
Find the adverbs and say which adjective each comes from
Narrate both labors
questions: What was special about the stag?
How long did Hercules chase the stag?
Where did the boar hide?
answers: It had golden horns and feet swifter than the wind

lessons.title: Lesson LVIII: Numerals; the Partitive Genitive
steps: Learn the cardinals 1–20, centum, ducentī, mīlle, and decline duo, trēs, mīlle (§ 479)
Learn the partitive genitive and why cardinals take ex or dē
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: What is the Latin for 12?
Translate: decem mīlia mīlitum
Write in Latin: one of my brothers

lessons.title: Reading LVIII: The Augean Stables and the Stymphalian Birds
steps: Translate the selection
Find the numerals in it
Tell how Hercules cleaned the stables in one day
questions: How many cattle did Augeas have?
How long had the stable gone uncleaned?
What did the Stymphalian birds have?

lessons.title: Lesson LIX: Ordinals and Distributives; the Accusative of Extent — Caesar in Gaul
steps: Learn the ordinals 1st–20th (§ 478) and singulī, bīnī, ternī
Learn the accusative of extent (how long? how far?) and sort the examples in § 336
Learn the vocabulary; translate Caesar in Gaul and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Vir tōtum diem cucurrit.
How many years did Caesar wage war in Gaul?
Write in Latin: the third legion
answers: The man ran for a whole day

lessons.title: Reading LIX: The Cretan Bull and the Horses of Diomedes
steps: Translate the two sections
Find an accusative of extent and an ablative of time
Narrate how Diomedes was punished
questions: How many days did Hercules sail to reach Crete?
How did Hercules seize the bull?
What did the horses eat?

lessons.title: Lesson LX: Deponent Verbs; Prepositions with the Accusative
steps: Learn the principal parts and synopses of hortor, vereor, sequor, patior, partior (§ 493)
Learn the prepositions with the accusative in § 340 and review those with the ablative
Learn the vocabulary; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Give the principal parts of sequor.
Translate: Imperātor eōs hortātus est.
What does deponent mean?
answers: Passive in form but active in meaning (it has laid aside its active forms)

lessons.title: Reading LX: The Belt of Hippolyte; Cerberus
steps: Translate the selection
Find the deponent verbs
Narrate the last labor and the end of Hercules
questions: Who wanted Hippolyte's belt?
How many heads did Cerberus have?
What did Jupiter finally give Hercules?

lessons.title: Review VII: Lessons LIII–LX
steps: Give the English of the words in § 524 and translate the list in § 525
Drill the words you missed
Answer the review questions on comparison, adverbs, numerals, and deponents
questions: Give the English of celeritās.
Give the Latin for "best."
Compare the adjective magnus.

units.title: Unit 9: The Subjunctive — The Story of Publius (Lessons LXI–LXV)

lessons.title: Lesson LXI: The Subjunctive Mood — the Present Subjunctive
steps: Read the introduction to Part III and § 342–343 on the four subjunctive tenses
Inflect the present subjunctive, active and passive, of all four conjugations and of sum (sim, sīs, sit)
Compare the indicative and subjunctive ideas in § 346 and do the exercise in § 347
questions: What is the mood sign of the present subjunctive in the first conjugation?
Translate: Statim proficīscāmur.
Give the present subjunctive, 3rd singular, of regō.
answers: Let us set out at once
lessons.notes: Part III begins here; the special vocabularies end, and review of the first 600 words takes their place.

lessons.title: Reading LXI: Publius Is Born near Pompeii
steps: Read the note on Roman names, then translate the selection
Find Vesuvius and Pompeii on a map
Describe the villa in English from the Latin
questions: What was the name of Publius's father?
Which mountain stood behind the villa?
How far away was Pompeii?

lessons.title: Lesson LXII: The Subjunctive of Purpose
steps: Learn the rule for purpose clauses and the words that introduce them: quī, ut, quō, nē
Study the four examples in § 351 and remember that Latin prose never uses the infinitive for purpose
Translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Fugiunt nē vulnerentur.
When is quō used to introduce a purpose clause?
Write in Latin: The Helvetii send ambassadors to seek peace.
answers: They flee so that they may not be wounded
When the clause contains a comparative
Helvētiī lēgātōs mittunt quī (ut) pācem petant

lessons.title: Reading LXII: His Life on the Farm
steps: Translate the selection
Find the purpose clauses (ut … gerant, nē tardī sint, quō … spectet)
Narrate a day of Publius and Lydia
questions: Who was the vīlicus of the farm?
Who was Publius's playmate?
Why could Publius's father not come home?
answers: He was waging wars for the state in faraway lands

lessons.title: Lesson LXIII: The Imperfect Subjunctive; Sequence of Tenses
steps: Form the imperfect subjunctive from the present infinitive, active and passive, and of sum (essem)
Learn the table of primary and secondary tenses (§ 357)
Translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Give the imperfect subjunctive, 3rd singular active, of audiō.
Which tenses of the indicative are secondary?
Write in Latin: He sent messengers to announce the victory.

lessons.title: Reading LXIII: Marcus Is Shipwrecked; Julia's Letter
steps: Read note 9 on how a Roman letter begins, then translate the letter
Find the purpose clauses and say why their verbs are imperfect
Write a three-line letter home using Sī valēs, bene est; ego valeō
questions: Where had Marcus been fighting?
For how many days was the ship driven by the storm?
From which city did Marcus write?

lessons.title: Lesson LXIV (Part 1): The Perfect and Pluperfect Subjunctive
steps: Inflect the perfect (-erim) and pluperfect (-issem) subjunctive active of the model verbs
Form the passives with sim and essem (amātus sim, amātus essem)
Inflect fuerim and fuissem, then the same tenses of cūrō, iubeō, sūmō
questions: How does the perfect subjunctive active differ from the future perfect indicative?
Give the pluperfect subjunctive, 3rd singular active, of regō.
Give the perfect subjunctive passive, 1st singular, of audiō.
answers: Only in the 1st singular: -erim instead of -erō

lessons.title: Lesson LXIV (Part 2): Substantive Clauses of Purpose
steps: Learn the rule: verbs of commanding, urging, asking, persuading, advising take ut/nē with the subjunctive
Learn the verb list in § 367 and the difference between iubeō (infinitive) and imperō (ut clause)
Translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Caesar Helvētiīs imperāvit nē per prōvinciam iter facerent.
Write in Latin with imperō: I order him to come.
Which verb of ordering takes the infinitive?
answers: Caesar ordered the Helvetii not to march through the province

lessons.title: Reading LXIV: Lentulus Reaches Home; a Trip to Pompeii
steps: Translate the selection
Find the clauses after suādet and hortātur
Describe what Publius saw in the streets of Pompeii
questions: At which harbor did Lentulus's ship land?
Why did Lentulus go to Pompeii?
By which gate did they enter the city?
answers: To buy fruit and food for a dinner with friends

lessons.title: Lesson LXV: The Subjunctive of possum; Verbs of Fearing
steps: Learn the subjunctive of possum (§ 495) and its accents
Learn why ut after a verb of fearing means "that not" and nē means "that" or "lest"
Translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Vereor ut hostium impetum sustinēre possim.
Write in Latin: We fear lest they are coming.
Give the present subjunctive, 3rd plural, of possum.
answers: I fear that I cannot withstand the enemy's attack

lessons.title: Reading LXV: A Day at Pompeii
steps: Translate the selection
Find the verb of fearing and the clauses after imperāvit
Read note 5 and explain how Romans counted the hours
questions: Where did they plan to buy cakes?
What did Publius want to stay and see?
What later destroyed the buildings of Pompeii?
answers: At the baker's shop by the lion-head fountain
The gladiator shows in the amphitheater
The fire and earthquake of Vesuvius

units.title: Unit 10: Participles, Irregular Verbs, and Result (Lessons LXVI–LXVIII)

lessons.title: Lesson LXVI (Part 1): The Participles — Forms
steps: Learn the four participles of each conjugation: present (-ns), future active (-ūrus), perfect passive, gerundive (-ndus)
Decline amāns and note -ī (adjective) versus -e (participle) in the ablative
Give the four participles of a deponent verb (hortāns, hortātūrus, hortātus, hortandus)
questions: Give the present active participle of capiō.
Give the future active participle of regō.
Which verbs have a perfect participle with active meaning?

lessons.title: Lesson LXVI (Part 2): Translating Participles
steps: Study the five model sentences in § 377 and say which conjunction (when, since, though) fits each
Translate Exercise I without translating the participles word for word
Put Exercise II into Latin, using participles for the clauses
questions: Translate: Oppidum captum vīdimus.
Translate: Sōl oriēns multōs interfectōs vīdit.
Write in Latin with a participle: frightened by the length of the way
answers: We saw the town which had been captured
The rising sun saw many slain

lessons.title: Reading LXVI: Lentulus Engages a Tutor for His Son
steps: Translate the selection
Find the relative clause of purpose (quī … docēret)
Read notes 9–10 and explain the bulla and the toga praetexta
questions: Who had taught Publius before the tutor came?
What language did the tutor teach besides music?
Where did the boys sit for lessons?
answers: In the peristyle of Marcus's house

lessons.title: Lesson LXVII (Part 1): The Irregular Verbs volō, nōlō, mālō
steps: Learn the principal parts and conjugation of volō, nōlō, mālō (§ 497)
Note the irregular present indicative, subjunctive, infinitive, and imperfect subjunctive
Do Exercise I, 1–4, and Exercise II, 1–3
questions: Translate: māvīs
Give the present infinitive of mālō.
Translate: Nōlīte!

lessons.title: Lesson LXVII (Part 2): The Ablative Absolute
steps: Study the four model sentences in § 380 and the rule in § 381
Read Notes 1–3 (tē duce; when not to use the construction; changing the voice)
Translate Exercise I, 5–13, and put Exercise II, 4–8, into Latin
questions: Translate: Hīs rēbus cognitīs, mīlitēs fūgērunt.
Translate: tē duce
Write in Latin: the Gauls having been conquered by Caesar (ablative absolute)
answers: When these things were learned, the soldiers fled

lessons.title: Reading LXVII: Publius Goes to Rome to Finish His Education
steps: Translate the selection, tracing the route on a map of Italy
Find each ablative absolute
List the towns Publius passed through on the Appian Way
questions: How old was Publius when he went to Rome?
Which famous orator welcomed them at Formiae?
How did travelers cross the great marshes?

lessons.title: Lesson LXVIII: The Irregular Verb fīō; the Subjunctive of Result
steps: Learn the principal parts and conjugation of fīō (§ 500), the passive of faciō
Learn result clauses with ut and ut nōn, and compare them with purpose clauses (§ 387)
Translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Terror erat tantus ut omnēs fugerent.
How does a negative result clause differ from a negative purpose clause?
Translate: fīet
answers: The terror was so great that all fled
Result uses ut nōn; purpose uses nē
It will happen (it will be made)

lessons.title: Reading LXVIII: Publius Puts On the Toga Virilis
steps: Translate the selection and Marcus's letter
Find the result clauses (ut … praebēret, ut … audīret)
Explain the difference between the toga praetexta and the toga virilis
questions: At what age did Publius put on the toga virilis?
What did Marcus dedicate to the household gods?
Where was Publius led after he put on the toga?

units.title: Unit 11: Characteristic, cum, Gerunds, Indirect Statement (Lessons LXIX–LXXII)

lessons.title: Lesson LXIX: The Subjunctive of Characteristic; the Predicate Accusative
steps: Study the four examples in § 389 and the difference between is quī dūcit and is quī dūcat
Learn the predicate accusative with verbs of making, choosing, and calling (creō, appellō, nōminō, vocō, faciō)
Translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Nihil videō quod timeam.
Write in Latin: The Romans made Caesar consul.
Write in Latin: These are not the men to betray their friends.
answers: Hī nōn sunt iī quī amīcōs suōs trādant

lessons.title: Reading LXIX: Publius Joins Caesar's Army in Gaul
steps: Translate the selection
Find the clause of characteristic (quī … praedīcerent) and the purpose clause with nē
Narrate how Publius got through the Gallic lines
questions: Which mountains did Publius cross?
How did he get past the Gauls?
What rank did Caesar give him?

lessons.title: Review VIII: Lessons LXI–LXIX
steps: Review the vocabularies of the first seventeen lessons (§§ 502, 503, 506, 507)
Answer the review questions in § 528 on the subjunctive, participles, and irregular verbs
Inflect the subjunctive of one verb of each conjugation, active and passive
questions: Name the four tenses of the subjunctive.
Which tenses are primary?
Give the participles of vereor.
answers: Present, future, future perfect (and perfect definite)

lessons.title: Lesson LXX: Constructions with cum; the Ablative of Specification
steps: Learn cum temporal, causal, and concessive, and when cum takes the indicative
Learn the ablative of specification and the idioms certiōrem facere, iter dare, obsidēs dare
Translate Exercise I, explaining each mood after cum, and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Homō erat corpore īnfīrmus sed validus animō.
What does cum mean with a concessive subjunctive?
Write in Latin: We shall inform Caesar.
answers: The man was weak in body but strong in courage

lessons.title: Reading LXX: The Rival Centurions
steps: Translate the story of Pullo and Vorenus
Find the cum clauses and say whether each is temporal, causal, or concessive
Narrate how the quarrel ended
questions: What were the two centurions' names?
What stopped Pullo from drawing his sword?
Which of them was judged braver?
answers: A weapon stuck in his belt pushed the scabbard aside
Neither; no one could judge between them

lessons.title: Lesson LXXI (Part 1): Vocabulary Review; the Gerund and Gerundive
steps: Review the word lists in §§ 510–511
Learn the gerund (amandī, amandō, amandum) and how it supplies the cases the infinitive lacks
Compare gerund and gerundive in § 405 and learn the purpose forms ad + accusative and genitive + causā
questions: Translate: Superandō Gallōs Caesar magnam glōriam reportāvit.
Write in Latin with the gerundive: the hope of making peace
Write in Latin with causā: They came to see the city.
answers: By overcoming the Gauls Caesar won great glory

lessons.title: Lesson LXXI (Part 2): The Predicate Genitive
steps: Learn the predicate genitive (equus est Galbae) and the idioms in § 410
Translate Exercise I, saying which forms are gerunds and which gerundives
Put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Iubēre est rēgīnae.
What does novīs rēbus studēre mean?
Write in Latin: These ornaments belong to Cornelia.
answers: To command is the queen's part (belongs to the queen)
To be eager for a revolution

lessons.title: Reading LXXI: The Enemy Besieging the Camp Are Repulsed
steps: Translate the selection
Find the gerund and the result clause in the same sentence
Narrate Publius's part in the battle
questions: How long had the battle lasted before Caesar ordered the sally?
Why could the soldiers not throw their spears?
How far did Publius chase the enemy?
answers: The enemy were too close; there was no room
To the Rhine, five miles away

lessons.title: Lesson LXXII (Part 1): The Irregular Verb eō and Its Compounds
steps: Learn the principal parts and conjugation of eō (§ 499)
Learn the compounds adeō, exeō, ineō, redeō, trānseō
Do Exercise I, 1–4
questions: Give the principal parts of eō.
Translate: ībunt
What does redeō mean?

lessons.title: Lesson LXXII (Part 2): Indirect Statements
steps: Compare English and Latin indirect statements (§§ 414–415)
Learn the rules for the accusative with infinitive and the tense of the infinitive
Learn the verbs of saying, knowing, thinking, perceiving; translate Exercise I, 5–14, and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Dīxit Gallōs fuisse fortīs.
Write in Latin: He says that the boy will be slow.
A future indicative in a direct statement becomes what in the indirect?
answers: He said that the Gauls had been brave

lessons.title: Reading LXXII: Publius Goes to Germany; Its Forests and Strange Animals
steps: Translate the selection
Find each indirect statement and turn one back into a direct statement
Describe the strange animals of the German forest
questions: Which lieutenant led the legions against the Germans?
What was said about the size of the great forest?
Why could the elk not get up if it fell?
answers: No one could cross it or knew its beginning or end

units.title: Unit 12: Final Constructions and Review (Lessons LXXIII–LXXIX)

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIII: Vocabulary Review; ferō; the Dative with Compounds
steps: Review the word lists in §§ 513–514
Learn the principal parts and conjugation of ferō (§ 498) and its compounds adferō, cōnferō, dēferō, īnferō, referō
Learn the dative with compound verbs and the idioms; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Give the principal parts of ferō.
Translate: Germānī Gallīs bellum īnferunt.
What does pedem referre mean?
answers: The Germans make war upon the Gauls

lessons.title: Reading LXXIII: The Storming of a City
steps: Translate the selection
List the Roman siege machines and say what each did
Draw a simple sketch of an agger with a tower and vineae
questions: How high was the wall of the town?
What were the vīneae for?
What did the battering rams do?
answers: To shelter soldiers as they came up to the wall
Broke down the wall and gates

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIV: Vocabulary Review; Indirect Questions
steps: Review the word lists in §§ 517–518
Compare direct and indirect questions (§ 431) and the use of num for whether
Learn the idioms; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Rogāvit ubi esset Rōma.
Write in Latin: He asks who is conquering the Gauls.
What does dē tertiā vigiliā mean?

lessons.title: Reading LXXIV: The City Is Taken; the Captives Are Questioned
steps: Translate the selection
Find the indirect questions
Narrate how the town fell
questions: Who gave the plan of attack in the council?
Whom had Caesar put in charge of the siege work?
At what time was the wall broken?

lessons.title: Lesson LXXV: Vocabulary Review; the Dative of Purpose
steps: Review the word lists in §§ 521–522
Learn the dative of purpose, often with a second dative (praesidiō castrīs)
Learn the idioms; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: Duās legiōnēs praesidiō castrīs relīquit.
Write in Latin: to choose a place for a camp
Translate: Hoc erat magnō impedīmentō Gallīs.
answers: He left two legions as a guard for the camp
This was a great hindrance to the Gauls

lessons.title: Reading LXXV: Civil War between Caesar and Pompey; the Battle of Pharsalia
steps: Translate the selection
Read the notes on the Rubicon and on Labienus
Find the dative of purpose (praesidiō castrīs) and narrate the battle
questions: Which river did Caesar cross to begin the civil war?
How large was Pompey's army compared with Caesar's?
Which line did Caesar send in to win the battle?
answers: His third line, kept fresh until then

lessons.title: Lesson LXXVI: Vocabulary Review; Genitive and Ablative of Description
steps: Review the word lists in §§ 524–525
Learn when description uses the genitive (measure) and when the ablative (physical traits)
Learn the idioms; translate Exercise I and put Exercise II into Latin
questions: Translate: fossa duodecim pedum
Write in Latin: a man with big feet and a small head
Translate: Helvētiīs in animō est.
